soil-hist-048.title: The Soil Science Society of America and its grand challenges
soil-hist-048.text: In 1936 two American groups decided they were stronger as one. The Soils Section of the American Society of Agronomy merged with the American Soil Survey Association. The result was the Soil Science Society of America, now the largest soil-specific scientific society in the United States. In 1934 that Soils Section had become the official Americas section of {{ref:soil-hist-047}}, a role the society still fills. From Madison, Wisconsin, it publishes journals, magazines and books, led by {{ref:soil-hist-078}}. Its voluntary certifications set standards for Certified Professional Soil Scientists and Certified Professional Soil Classifiers. In 2011 it named the field's grand challenges: climate change, food and energy security, waste treatment and water quality, and human and ecosystem health. In 2017 it stretched its definition of soil to loose material at or near any planetary surface. Past presidents include William Albrecht in 1939, Hans Jenny in 1949 and Rattan Lal in 2007. Its outreach runs from the 'Secrets of Soil' exhibition at the Smithsonian to the school websites Soils4Teachers and soils4kids.

soil-hist-050.title: From Dust Bowl emergency to a national conservation agency
soil-hist-050.text: The agency was born in a crisis. On September 13, 1933, the Department of the Interior formed the Soil Erosion Service, with {{ref:soil-hist-019}} as chief. Bennett knew the soil erosion behind the 1930s Dust Bowl, and he stayed in charge until he retired in 1952. On March 23, 1935, the service moved to the Department of Agriculture and soon merged with other units as the Soil Conservation Service. Between 1933 and 1942 it ran 500 Civilian Conservation Corps camps, mainly for erosion control, and promoted contour plowing. In 1994 it became the Natural Resources Conservation Service, a USDA agency that gives technical help to farmers and other private landowners. Its money for farmers and ranchers comes through the Farm Bill, renewed every five years. It leads {{ref:soil-hist-051}}, with products such as the Web Soil Survey and the SSURGO database. Since 2015 it has also pushed soil health, with less tillage and more cover crops.

soil-hist-053.title: Rothamsted, where wheat has grown in one field since 1843
soil-hist-053.text: One field in Harpenden, England, has been sown with winter wheat every year since 1843. That is the Broadbalk Experiment at Rothamsted, one of the world's oldest agricultural research institutions. John Bennet Lawes, who had founded an early artificial fertilizer factory, set it up on his estate to test how fertilizers affect crop yields. With Joseph Henry Gilbert, trained under Liebig, he ran field trials for 57 years. They laid the foundations of scientific agriculture and crop nutrition. Thomas Way and Lawes discovered cation exchange there, and in 1878 Robert Warington confirmed soil nitrification. The mountain of data had a further payoff. Ronald Fisher, hired in 1919 to analyse it, stayed to create the theory of experimental design. Merged into the Institute of Arable Crops Research in 1987, the station now runs as Rothamsted Research.

soil-hist-047.title: How the world's soil scientists organized in 1924
soil-hist-047.text: Soil scientists from many nations met in Rome in 1924 and founded the International Society of Soil Science. Today it is the International Union of Soil Sciences, the field's international scientific union and a member of the International Science Council. Its aim is to promote every branch of {{ref:soil-found-090}}, link soil scientists and spur research and its use. It has 86 national and regional member societies with about 60,000 scientists, plus individual members in 57 countries. Every four years it holds the World Congress of Soil Science; the first met in Washington, D.C., in 1927. Its commissions, grown from six in 1924, cover soil morphology, fertility, degradation control, education and the field's own history. It endorses the World Reference Base as the international standard for soil classification. Since 2014 its Council has elected the President for a two-year term. Since January 2023 Italy's Council for Agricultural Research and Economics has run its secretariat.

soil-hist-051.title: The National Cooperative Soil Survey maps a nation's soils
soil-hist-051.text: The first American soil surveys cost about 3/10ths of a cent per acre; by 1999 a survey cost about $3 an acre. Behind that work stands the National Cooperative Soil Survey. It is a nationwide partnership that investigates, inventories, classifies and interprets US soils and publishes the results. The {{ref:soil-hist-050}} leads it, joining federal land agencies, state agricultural experiment stations, counties and conservation districts. Land-grant universities have been partners from the start, and Cooperative Extension joins them today. Federal authority comes from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896. The work passed from an 1894 Division of Agricultural Soil to the Bureau of Soils in 1901, and to the Soil Conservation Service in 1952. Its maps judge land capability and conservation needs. More than 90% of private lands have been mapped, and in FY2001 maps were made or updated for 21,900,000 acres. The soil series it establishes form one level of {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-hist-049.title: ISRIC, the world's data center for soils
soil-hist-049.text: ISRIC began in 1966 on the advice of the International Society of Soil Science, now the IUSS, and UNESCO. It is an independent, science-based foundation that supplies quality-assessed soil information for global environmental and social challenges. It writes soil information standards, builds harmonised global soil products and strengthens national and regional {{ref:soil-agri-085}}. Since 1989 it has been the accredited World Data Centre for Soils. Its flagship products are WoSIS and SoilGrids. It also houses the World Soil Museum and the World Soil Reference Collection, and its Otto Spaargaren helped draft the World Reference Base.

soil-found-104.title: Pochvovedenie, the Russian journal of soil science
soil-found-104.text: Pochvovedenie is a Russian journal of soil science, read abroad in English translation as Eurasian Soil Science. Its pages carried an early argument about the field's own origins. In a 1904 article there, its editor Arseny Yarilov, the bibliographer of Russian soil science, hailed Fallou as the founder of soil science.

soil-hist-057.title: The Soil Science Society of Poland
soil-hist-057.text: In 1937 Feliks Terlikowski, Jan Włodek and Tadeusz Mieczyński founded the society of Polish soil scientists, the Polskie Towarzystwo Gleboznawcze. It promotes soil science, pedology, agricultural chemistry and agricultural microbiology in Poland. In 2017 it had about 450 members in 14 regional and 4 thematic divisions. A member of the IUSS, it publishes Soil Science Annual, founded in 1950 as Roczniki Gleboznawcze. It also produces {{ref:soil-class-034}}, whose 5th edition appeared in 2011 and 6th in 2019.

soil-hist-052.title: How the United States began mapping its soils
soil-hist-052.text: American soil survey began with $16,000. Milton Whitney started field work on May 3, 1899, mapping about 720,000 acres that year in tobacco lands and alkali areas. The first surveyors, geologists or chemists, split soils mainly by texture and grouped soil types into series. {{ref:soil-hist-009}}, in charge from 1913, drew on Glinka's Russian school. He came to treat soil science as separate from geology and to describe soils by horizons. After years of clashes over methods, all USDA survey work was consolidated under the Soil Conservation Service in 1952.

soil-hist-055.title: The International Humic Substances Society and its reference samples
soil-hist-055.text: Coal, soil and water scientists share an interest in the same dark organic matter. On September 11, 1981, in Denver, Colorado, they founded the International Humic Substances Society to study it. The society researches natural organic matter in soil and water, the {{ref:soil-chem-058}} at its core. It keeps standard samples of humic and fulvic acids from leonardite, river water, a mineral soil and peat. Scientists in about 40 countries use them. It also backs standard lab methods and holds biennial conferences. As of 2023 it had about 450 members in 24 chapters.

soil-hist-078.title: The Soil Science Society of America Journal
soil-hist-078.text: The Soil Science Society of America Journal is the bimonthly, peer-reviewed flagship of {{ref:soil-hist-048}}, covering every aspect of soil science. It began in 1937 as Soil Science Society of America Proceedings, with J. D. Luckett as founding editor. It took its present title in 1973. Since 2013 it has appeared only online, and its articles undergo double-blind review, so neither authors nor reviewers know each other's names.

soil-found-113.title: The Journal of Soil and Water Conservation
soil-found-113.text: Conservation is a science, a practice and a policy, and one journal covers all three. The Journal of Soil and Water Conservation is a bimonthly, peer-reviewed journal on {{ref:soil-agri-059}} and the protection of water. The Soil and Water Conservation Society publishes it.

soil-hist-056.title: ICOMANTH and the soils that people make
soil-hist-056.text: From 1995 to 2013 a committee worked on a question older systems had skirted: how to classify soils made by human activity. It was the International Committee on Anthropogenic Soils, or ICOMANTH. Ray Bryant chaired it at its founding, and John Galbraith succeeded him in 2004. According to the NRCS, its main contribution was better standards for describing these soils and defining the taxa to classify them. The NRCS judged its task complete. In 2014 several of its proposals entered {{ref:soil-class-006}}.

soil-hist-054.title: The European Soil Bureau Network
soil-hist-054.text: Europe's soil problems cross borders, from agrochemical leaching and heavy metals to waste disposal, erosion and lost soil structure. In 1996 the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra created the European Soil Bureau Network to meet them. It links national soil science institutions as 'Centres of Excellence' that collect and harmonise soil information for Europe. Staff of the JRC's Land Management Unit run it and host its secretariat. They give the Commission a central source of soil information, feeding {{ref:soil-found-069}}.

openers.societies-institutes-and-journals: Science needs places to meet, publish and keep records, and soil science built many. Rothamsted, founded in 1843 at Harpenden, England, is one of the oldest agricultural research institutions in the world. In 1924 soil scientists founded an international society, and in 1936 Americans formed the Soil Science Society of America. Survey agencies, data centers and specialist societies followed, along with peer-reviewed journals in several languages. This chapter tours the institutions that keep the field running.

reviews.societies-institutes-and-journals: Soil science runs on institutions as well as ideas. Rothamsted's long-term field trials, begun in 1843, gave the field data, cation exchange and modern experimental design. American survey work grew from Whitney's first mapping in 1899 into the National Cooperative Soil Survey, led by the agency Bennett founded during the Dust Bowl. Worldwide, the IUSS links national societies from America to Poland, and ISRIC, which it helped create, keeps the world's soil data. Journals from Pochvovedenie to the Soil Science Society of America Journal, and committees like ICOMANTH, carry the results into classification and practice.
